title: Sustainable Labs Interest Session
description:
Campus labs and research are incredibly important to the University, but they're also very water and energy intensive. In fact, campus labs are the largest consumers of water and energy on campus. Started in 2009 as the Green Labs program, Sustainable Carolina has revamped the program and given it a new name: Sustainable Labs.

 

The program focuses on key areas (waste, energy and water, freezers, chemicals), and is designed not to shame labs or lab personnel for waste or energy intensive equipment, but rather to identify small steps labs can take to be more sustainable and to recognize all the steps that labs have already taken.

 

This interest session for Sustainable Labs will be led by Langley Smith, Sustainable Carolina’s program specialist. We invite lab managers, students who work in labs, and faculty to join us and learn how their labs can participate in the program.

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Experience the Experimental Engineering Lab
description:
Step inside the Experimental Engineering Lab (EEL) in the Department of Computer Science, one of UNC-Chapel Hill’s most unique research environments, and discover how researchers and students turn ambitious ideas into working technologies.

 

Locations and projects to be displayed:

Room SN244, Robotics and Autonomous Vehicles: Biologically driven autonomous vehicles and PAWS, an assistive navigation robot.Room SN236, COMP 290 Course and the Machine Shop: Conversations with students and lessons on how fabrication and welding turn research ideas into working devices.Room FB241, Virtual Reality, Augmented Reality, and Holograms: Interactive showcases of boundary-aware redirected walking in virtual reality, mixed-reality motorcycle assembly training, and floating holographic displays.Room SN247, Fluids, Movement, and Perception: Demonstrations of finger-position optimization for swimming, a hand position tracking glove, and augmented aurality. 

The Experimental Engineering Lab supports research that blends computing with hands-on engineering, providing access to spaces and tools rarely found within a computer science department, including machine shops, electronics fabrication facilities, rapid prototyping labs, wet labs, and specialized testing environments. Students and researchers use the lab to develop everything from robotics and virtual reality experiences to health technologies and environmental monitoring tools.

 

This is an in-person event.

 

As part of UNC Research Week and in partnership with Carolina Performing Arts, this open house invites UNC and Chapel Hill community members to explore the lab through 10+ demonstrations and conversations with Carolina researchers and students.

 

This “Open Laboratory” concept offers a preview of what attendees can experience at Carolina Performing Arts’ upcoming All. Together. Now. festival (February 19–21), which will bring together artists, scholars, and communities. Through interactive experiences and informal discussions, festival participants will discover how research, creativity, and collaboration can deepen our understanding of the world and inspire new possibilities for the future.

Whether you’re curious about emerging technologies, interested in the creative process, or simply looking for a behind-the-scenes look at research happening on campus, we invite you to participate in UNC Research Week by visiting the EEL Lab to experience innovation in action.

title: Mike Wiley: One Noble Journey
description:
FEATURING

Mike Wiley

Mike Wiley holds a Masters of Fine Arts from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and was the 2010 and 2014 Lehman Brady Visiting Joint Chair Professor in Documentary Studies and American Studies at Duke University and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Wiley received the University of North Carolina’s Distinguished Alumni Award in 2017.

 

PROGRAM

One Noble Journey

Henry “Box” Brown was an African American born into slavery in 1816 in Louisa County, Virginia. Although he was not subjected to physical violence, Henry’s story (the basis for One Noble Journey) demonstrates the cruelty of slavery was every bit as devastating to the heart as it could be on the body.After his family was torn apart and parceled out to various beneficiaries of the estate, Henry devised an ingenious escape plan – sealing himself in a wooden box for shipment to friends and freedom in Philadelphia.

One Noble Journey also recounts the daring and miraculous quest for freedom of Elizabeth Craft and her husband William, who were born into slavery in Georgia.* Ellen Craft, who was very light skinned, disguised herself as a sickly, white gentleman traveling to Philadelphia for medical treatment. Ellen and William, who acted as her slave throughout the journey, bravely traveled on public trains and steamers as they made their way up the eastern seaboard to Philadelphia. Eventually they were forced to sail for England after the Fugitive Slave Law enabled slave hunters to pursue them even in free states.

 

PARKING

Please plan to arrive early as parking on campus can be tricky. Learn more about parking and directions to UNC-Chapel Hill’s campus.

title: Narrative of a Slave Woman: Songs of Hope, Justice, and Freedom
description:
FEATURING

LaToya Lain, soprano

 

PROGRAM

A powerful presentation by soprano LaToya Lain that examines the issue of slavery by combining musical performance with spoken narrative accounts. About the project, Lain says, “In 2003, HBO presented a documentary entitled ‘Unchained Memories’ about the stories of former slaves interviewed during the 1930s’ Federal Writers’ Project. As I read the print version of these slave narratives and later watched the documentary, I began to see how the stories of these men and women are told through the Negro Spirituals. I saw the direct relationship of some of my favorite spirituals and the life stories of remarkable slave women, whose names, if not for these narratives, we would have never known. I was inspired to take these narratives and combine them with concert arranged Negro Spirituals to tell the story of one former slave woman through song.”

 

PARKING

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words
description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026

This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

 

An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.

Refreshments will be served.

Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

**There will be a second celebration of this exhibit on Friday, October 9 (5-7pm) in honor of the 246th Commemoration Weekend of this historical event.**

title: Native Tree Planting (Cornelius)
description:
Join NCWF Lake Norman Wildlife Chapter to plant native trees in Cornelius as part of North Carolina Wildlife Federation’s Clean and Green program. Back in April, NCWF Lake Norman Wildlife Chapter and the Town of Cornelius hosted its annual Clean & Green trash cleanup event. Town staff and volunteers from the Society of Women Engineers, Safe Harbor – Kings Point Marina, and Lake Norman Wildlife took to the land and the lake to remove hundreds of pounds of trash and debris. 
North Carolina Wildlife Federation is committed to planting one native tree for every 25 pounds of trash collected statewide. Removing litter protects wildlife from possible entanglement, strangulation, and ingestion while improving water quality and removing toxins from the environment. 
This year we will plant native trees at Bailey Road Park. Trees are the foundation of our terrestrial food webs, and they provide critical nesting habitat for owls, hawks, songbirds, and other wildlife. Please join us at Bailey Road Park for a morning of community and conservation. Stick around for pizza, refreshments, and a group photo at the end. 
Volunteers will work to prepare the existing holes before planting and mulching up to 80 native trees. 
Children under 18 must be accompanied by a parent or guardian. 
Please reach out to Billy Wilson, President – Lake Norman Wildlife, with questions at billy.wilson@LNWC.org, or 704-675-2011

title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence
description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.

The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

Visit 5 Points Gallery in person or online at https://5pointsgallery.com. All work from the exhibition is available for shipping or pickup. title: Open Studio: Glass & Other
location: Fusion Gallery, 321 W Main St, Durham, 27701, United States
description:
Drop in and create on your own terms! Your Open Studio Day Pass gives you access to Fusion Gallery’s shared studio space from 1:00 PM–7:00 PM on your selected day. Come in anytime after 1:00 PM and stay as late as 7:00 PM. 
Use our studio space and tools or bring your own project to work on; perfect for artists who don’t have a home studio or simply want dedicated time and space to make. Personal cubbies are also available to store works-in-progress between visits. 
Online registration or sign-up via email is required before coming in. Drop-ins are not permitted at this time. If you’d like to come in at a time you don’t see available online, email us at info@fusionnc.com. 
How Open Studio Works
Open Studio is self-guided and does not include instruction. You should already have the skills needed to safely work in your chosen medium. It’s also a great opportunity to finish projects started during a Fusion class. 
Your Day Pass includes access to our shared workspace, tools, equipment, and currently available non-consumable materials. Consumable and specialty materials are charged separately based on usage. 
Stained & Fused Glass
Prior stained or fused glass experience is required to use our glass tools. Taking a basics or beginner class at Fusion is recommended, but previous instruction at Carolina Stained Glass or Say It With Glass is also accepted. 
• Glass, solder, foil, and frit: $35/lb
• Bringing your own stained glass? Foil and solder use: $6
• Paper stained glass patterns: Free
• Vinyl-cut patterns: $3 each
• An assortment of stained glass patterns is available for studio use
• Kiln firings are handled by Fusion staff only 
Silver Clay
Prior silver clay experience is required to use silver clay tools. Taking a beginner class at Fusion is recommended before using the studio independently. 
• Silver clay: $7/gram prior to firing
• Firing of your completed piece is included and will be completed at the convenience of Fusion studio staff
• Guests may not fire their own pieces without prior authorization from Fusion’s owners 
Drawing & Painting
No prior class or experience is required for drawing or painting. Your Open Studio fee includes access to currently available shared drawing and painting materials. 
Please Note
• Day Pass access is valid 1:00 PM–7:00 PM on your selected date only
• Online or email registration is required before arriving—no walk-ins
• Open Studio is self-guided and does not include instruction
• Some specialty tools, equipment, or processes may require prior approval or demonstrated experience
• Guests are responsible for cleaning their workspace and helping maintain a respectful shared environment
• Misuse of the space, tools, or equipment or failure to follow studio guidelines may result in removal from the studio without refund

title: Words and Motion: Poetry in Translation
description:
Duke English and the Duke Writers Collective invite you to a bilingual poetry reading at Duke Coffee House on Saturday, October 24th, from 7-8 PM at the Duke Coffee House. Words and Motion: Poetry in Translation brings writers Tsitsi Jaji and Crystal Simone Smith together with poet-translator duo Claire Cullen and Joann Woo.  Moving among languages, histories, and forms, the night's readers will consider writing not only as something that can be translated, but as an act of translation itself-a bridge between experience, place, and mind.  Light refreshments served. 
Bios:
Claire Cullen and Joann Woo are the co-presidents of the Duke Writers' Collective (DWC), a close community of writers at Duke University where writers meet, share, and grow in their personal creative endeavors. Along with snacks, DWC offers weekly writing hours, community-building events, and outreach workshops in Durham public schools. 
 
Crystal Simone Smith is the author of several collections of poetry, Common Sense (1776), Addressed to the Citizens of Today: An Erasure (Beacon Press, 2026), Runagate: Songs of the Freedom Bound (Duke University Press, 2025), winner of the Roanoke-Chowan Poetry Award, and Dark Testament (Henry Holt, 2023). In 2022, her haiku collection, Ebbing Shore, won The Haiku Foundation Touchstone Distinguished Book Award. Smith is the recipient of a Duke Humanities Unbounded Fellowship. Her work has appeared in numerous journals including POETRY Magazine, Harper's Magazine, Rattle, Frogpond, and Modern Haiku. She teaches in the Thompson Writing Program at Duke University and writes poetry about the human condition and social change.
 
Tsitsi Jaji teaches English and African & African American Studies at Duke University, where she is Helen L. Bevington Associate Professor of Modern Poetry. She is a senior research associate at Rhodes University. Her books include the award-winning monograph Africa in Stereo: Music, Modernism and Pan-African Solidarity, two volumes of poetry, Mother Tongues and Beating the Graves, and the chapbook Carnaval. Several of her poems have been set to music, and her collaboration with Shawn Okpebholo, Songs in Flight, was nominated for a 2025 Grammy. She specializes in not quite making it, but she's happy being a runner-up.

description:
It's time to play the third annual Cyber Bowl, a month-long competition to determine which North Carolina university is the most cyber savvy.

UNC-Chapel Hill faces off against nine other North Carolina universities with a lot to prove and two wins to defend. title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words
description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026

This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

 

An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.

Refreshments will be served.

Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

**There will be a second celebration of this exhibit on Friday, October 9 (5-7pm) in honor of the 246th Commemoration Weekend of this historical event.**

title: Shia Islamic-Jewish Legal Reasoning in Dialogue
description:
Over the last four years, the Shia Islamic-Jewish Legal Reasoning in Dialogue has brought together 13 scholars from across the U.S. and internationally to study legal texts of both traditions via diverse methodologies of academic analysis. They have been divided  into 6 working groups working on the topics of the legal self, constitutionalism, theocracy, language, female clerical authority, and the persecution of heretics. The Dialogue is not merely meant to identify similarities and differences, but to allow scholars to think their "own" tradition conceptually anew through this encounter. The project arrives at Duke in order to present its findings and receive constructive critique from Triangle-area scholars of co-written book chapters that will eventually be published in Rutgers University Press' "Transmodern Times" series.

More information at: 
https://jewishstudies.duke.edu/shia-islamic-jewish-legal-reasoning-dialogue

title: Vintage Rides Ride
description:
Carolina Tarwheels Cycling Club
What is a Vintage Rides Ride? Well, it's where we pull out the old bikes and remember (or imagine) what it was like in the old days, when bikes were (mostly) steel, tires were skinny, jerseys were wool, and pedals had toe clips ("toe cages" to you younger folks). Shifters were generally on the down tube, and friction operated- no one had to charge any batteries before the ride. So bring your classics, or ride anything at all, but come along for a relaxed, easy ride. All riders and all bikes are welcome!
Route here:
[https://ridewithgps.com/routes/39713600](https://ridewithgps.com/routes/39713600) or something similar.
**Route subject to change at the leader's whim** (often based on what kind of gearing we're on). Distance approximately 20 miles. We will regroup if necessary, so no one will be left out there.

It is Tarwheels policy for all riders to sign the ride waiver before coming out to the ride.

\*\*\* WAIVER \*\*\* http://tarwheels.net/ewaiver
MEMBERS need only do this ONCE a YEAR. NON-MEMBERS are required to do this before EACH RIDE, please consider becoming a member.

description:

title: ADULT FORUM - "The Gown Speaks First: What the Church Hears BEFORE a Sermon Begins"
description:
Before a preacher reaches the sermon's first sentence, a congregation is already learning whom to trust. A Geneva gown. A rhinestoned stole. A preacher's voice breaking into song. Each can teach a room what authority is supposed to look and sound like-and who seems strangely out of place. Drawing on his recently published article in the Journal of the American Academy of Religion, Brett McKinley Pardue brings Christian vesture into conversation with drag performance and the visual and sonic life of worship. What does preaching communicate before words-and what if faithful authority arrives dressed differently than we expect?

The Congregation's weekly Adult Forum offers a variety of guest speakers, presentations and discussions on a wide range of thought-provoking topics, including Biblical studies, current social issues and the work of mission agencies.  Adult Forum aims to deepen the faith and understanding of adults through shared learning experiences. Classes include programs and discussions on contemporary issues in light of Christian teachings.

title: University Worship
description:
Join us in worship that offers stirring preaching, inspiring sacred music, and faithful prayer. Held year-round amid the beautiful, soaring architecture of Duke Chapel, this interdenominational Christian service is characterized by vibrant faith, intellectual depth, diverse cultural expressions, and a welcoming community.

All are welcome at this service. To attend a service, navigate to 125 Science Drive, Durham, NC. Parking is available at that address in the Bryan Center Garage with ADA parking in the adjacent surface lot. Parking in the garage is free on Sunday until 2:00 p.m. when using the standard ticket issued upon entering the garage. Regular attendees of the service are encouraged to receive a pass for free parking on Sunday mornings at the visitor desk inside the Chapel.

Resources for the service:
* Make an offering online: https://chapel.duke.edu/offering
* View an online version of the hymnal here: https://hymnary.org/hymnal/UMH

A national leader in the theological study of the art of preaching, Chapel Dean Luke A. Powery preaches regularly at this service, along with a rotation of other Chapel ministers and renowned guest preachers. The acclaimed Duke Chapel Choir and Chapel organists lead the music, supplemented by student chamber groups, professional instrumentalists, and visiting artists.

Services are streamed live on YouTube and broadcast live on channel 12 of the Duke Hospital TV system and on the radio on 620 AM WDNC. Subscribe to the Duke Chapel Sermons podcast on Spotify or Apple Podcasts. Find an archive of Chapel sermons on our website and a more extensive digital archive in the Duke Chapel Recordings collection on the Duke Libraries website.

For a listing of Christian education offerings held before the service, see the Duke Chapel website calendar.

The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

title: CEE Seminar - Understanding and Computation of Deformation and Failure in Porous Microstructures
description: This talk presents a body of work aimed at closing that gap, premised on the idea that a sharper physical understanding of how porous solids fail is what enables good approximations of it. Mechanical stress in a loaded microstructure concentrates at the geometric constrictions of the solid, which we hypothesize to be the preferred sites for cracks to nucleate under most loads. This is the basis for a reduced-order model that foreshadows where cracks form and thereby gains several orders of magnitude in computational speed. This hypothesis, which was first supported by phase-field simulations, is now being confirmed by in-situ tensile experiments on 3D-printed porous specimens. Underlying these approximations is a pore-level multiscale method (PLMM) that decomposes the solid into subdomains with local, physics-based closures. We discuss a geometric formulation of it that allows cracks to take arbitrary trajectories, overcoming the limitations of the reduced-order model. We then recast PLMM as an algebraic preconditioner, so it accelerates existing finite-element and finite-volume codes by over an order of magnitude relative to algebraic multigrid. The preconditioner retains rigorous error control and handles both pre-existing and evolving cracks. We also discuss a high-order variant that captures bending- and torsion-dominated loads, the use of machine learning to lower the cost of building the preconditioner, and ongoing extensions to plasticity and large-strain deformations. PLMM originated in pore-scale flow, exploiting the constrictions of the void space to outperform pore-network models. Only recently have the above ideas for mechanics enabled its geometric formulation to be recast as a preconditioner for the Navier-Stokes equations. The talk weighs trade-offs of these accelerations and points to current gaps, including fluid-induced failure and upscaling to Darcy scale.

title: What's a Libertarian, and Might You Be One? A Conversation with Katherine Mangu-Ward
description:
An "Independent Thinkers" Conversation with Katherine Mangu-Ward hosted by Frank Bruni, Duke professor and New York Times columnist
Oct. 26, 6 p.m., Penn Pavilion

Few people's ideologies are wholly and neatly represented by the Democratic or Republican party. But what else is there? What's the meaning of a different label? And is wearing one a route out of the country's ruinous partisanship?

Please join Frank Bruni for a spirited conversation - part of his "Independent Thinkers" series of events - with Katherine Mangu-Ward, the editor in chief of Reason magazine, which is the country's leading libertarian journal.

Mangu-Ward not only holds the top job at Reason, the magazine of "free minds and free markets," but also has written many of its cover stories, including one that defended plastic bags and another that made a case for not voting, and appears on its weekly podcast. She has contributed to The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post; did a TED Talk about what capitalism gets right (and government gets wrong); and has been spotlighted on many television shows, including HBO's Real Time with Bill Maher. 

Frank Bruni teaches at Duke's Sanford School of Public Policy as part of the DeWitt Wallace Center for Media and Democracy. He's also a longtime writer for The New York Times and the author of five bestselling books.

Frank's "Independent Thinkers" conversations with public figures who defy reductive political labels are part of the Provost's Initiative on Pluralism, Free Inquiry and Belonging.

title: Trick & Meet: A Very Scary Singles Mixer (20s-30s)
description:

Are you a Morticia looking for your Gomez? Maybe you're Chucky looking for his Tiffany! Jack Skellingtons and Sallys come one and all to find your doomed duo.

Spooky season is here, and we wanna run it back for everyone else! 👻

Join Triangle Third Place and Discover Durham Together at Drink a Bull in Durham for a mixer filled with tea, cocktails, mocktails, new connections, and just enough Halloween chaos.

**🎃 Come in costume, add a little spooky flair, or just show up as yourself... there is no requirement.**

🟢**Spooky Bingo**

What's the best way to learn something you didn’t know before? Bingo, obviously. Walk around and check off some boxes, chat with new friends, or lovers and win a super secret dark prize!

☕ **Spill the Tea**

Who doesn't like some Tea? We’ll also have an anonymous Spill the Tea jar circulating throughout the evening.

Drop in a confession, unpopular opinion, ridiculous dating story, queer awakening, Halloween hot take, or harmless secret. Throughout the night, we’ll pull a few out and expose them.

No names. No judgment. Potentially a little chaos.

🐂 **Drink a Bull**

Drink a Bull serves both specialty teas and alcoholic beverages, so whether your potion of choice is boozy, caffeinated, or completely alcohol-free, there’s something for you.

🚗 Plenty of parking around the building, but if it fills up you can park at Dollar General and walk over
💕 A little singles mixer etiquette (with love!) 😂
We’re excited to bring everyone together for a fun, relaxed night of meeting new people, making connections, and maybe finding a little chemistry! ✨
To help keep things comfortable and fun for everyone, just a few friendly reminders:

* Flirting is welcome! Just make sure the interest is mutual. 😉
* Respect boundaries. If someone’s not interested, no hard feelings! There are plenty of new people to meet.
* Remember, being friendly doesn’t automatically mean someone is flirting.
* Be kind and respectful to everyone, whether there’s romantic interest or not.
* Don’t be shy about starting a conversation! That’s why we’re all here. 💕

Most importantly, we’re a community first and a singles mixer second. We want everyone to leave feeling comfortable, respected, and happy they came!
If anything makes you uncomfortable, please find a host. We’re here to help. 💛
Be yourself. Be respectful. Keep the creepy vibes at home. 😂💕
Come for the company. Stay for the chemistry. 😉

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words
description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026

This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

 

An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.

Refreshments will be served.

Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

**There will be a second celebration of this exhibit on Friday, October 9 (5-7pm) in honor of the 246th Commemoration Weekend of this historical event.**

title: CDVS Workshop: Sharing Human Participants Data: Challenges and (Potential) Solutions
description: The sharing of research data has become increasingly important to federal and private funders and journal publishers for a number of reasons (research transparency, reproducibility, return on investment, new research on existing data, etc.). With the latest requirements from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) for Data Management and Sharing Plans (https://sharing.nih.gov/), there are legitimate concerns about how data from human beings can ethically and safely be shared. This workshop will talk about the various challenges that arise when considering how to share human participants data in DMSPs and potential ways that these challenges can be addressed, and even solved, with resources available at Duke and beyond (data sharing consent language, controlled access repositories, de-identification help, etc.). This event is open to non-Duke participants. This workshop is eligible for 2 hours of Graduate School RCR Credit (GS714) and 200-level faculty and staff RCR.

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

During our ecoEXPLORE “Shifting Species” program, NCWF, Pocosin Lakes National Wildlife Refuge, and Tyrrell County Library will dive into how species shift their behavior in response to changes in weather vs. climate as we work to complete our Climate Badge Challenge 3! Join us as we learn more about local and regional examples of wildlife and plants that have adapted due to changes in their environment. 
To celebrate the end of the Arachnology Field Season, ecoEXPLORErs are invited to wear their arachnid costumes from the Arachnology Badge Challenge 3! Don’t feel like dressing up? That’s okay, we’d love to see a sketch of your costume design instead! 
ecoEXPLORE is a community science program, created by the North Carolina Arboretum, where children of all ages are able to learn how to identify wildlife around them, help real scientists track wildlife activity, and earn fun badges and prizes all at the same time! To learn more about ecoEXPLORE, please visit https://www.ecoexplore.net/.

title: Building Partnerships for Innovation: A Fireside Chat with Vice Chancellor Tommy Sowers
description:
Join Innovate Carolina for a fireside conversation with Tommy Sowers, Vice Chancellor for Innovation, Entrepreneurship and Economic Development at UNC Chapel Hill, about UNC's role in building stronger partnerships across North Carolina and supporting innovation and economic development in the region. Hosted at 79°West in Pittsboro, the conversation will focus on the growing opportunities to connect UNC with communities, entrepreneurs and North Carolina based companies throughout Central North Carolina. 

 

Chatham County and Pittsboro are an important part of this regional ecosystem, creating opportunities for UNC to build stronger relationships with the communities and companies surrounding the university. The conversation will also highlight UNC's Industry Partnerships Initiative and its focus on developing meaningful relationships with North Carolina companies. Together, these partnerships can connect companies with UNC's talent, research, innovation and entrepreneurial resources while creating opportunities for greater economic impact across the state. 

 

Come hear Vice Chancellor Sowers share his perspective on Carolina's role in the region, the opportunities ahead for Central North Carolina, and how stronger partnerships can benefit both the university and the communities around it.

title: Trail Tuesday night ride....casual style ... at Williamson Preserve
description:
Triangle Off Road Cyclists (TORC)
***PLEASE CHECK https://www.trianglemtb.com/ FOR TRAIL STATUS.***\*

If the trail is closed the ride is canceled.
\*\*\*\*BRING LIGHTS!!!!!!!!!!\*\*\*\*\*\*\*

This is NOT a true beginner mountain biker friendly ride.

This is a good ride for those new to night riding or those who just want to check it out.

This is a **casual** no drop ride for riders who want to ride and socialize. This is not a race or a Strava KOM fest.

We normally split into 2 groups if there are enough riders.... a casual group and a super casual group.
Both groups will be no drop and will stop to regroup often to ensure no one is left behind.

We will meet between 5:30-5:45pm and hit the trail at 6:00pm.
We hang out to chitchat after the ride ... (sometimes with hot cocoa and baked goods) so come for the ride, stay for the laughs (and cocoa).

**Traffic sucks on the way to Williamson so give yourself more time to get there then you think you will need. Please be ready to ride at 6:00pm**

We will meet at the white barn on the opposite side of the church from the main trail head parking lot. Parking here is by special permission for the ride. (Parking here without special permission from TLC is not allowed and considered trespassing so please only park here with TLC's permission.)

PLEASE SEE THE LINK BELOW FOR PARKING. DO NOT PARK AT THE REGULAR PARKING LOT.

https://www.google.com/maps/place/35%C2%B043'57.9%22N+78%C2%B026'54.0%22W/@35.7327613,-78.4505187,17z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x0:0x0!7e2!8m2!3d35.7327571!4d-78.4483296

Mountain bike, helmet, and light are required.
NO ONE CAN RIDE WITHOUT A HELMET.
Gloves, water bottle/pack, mini-tool, spare tube, and pump/CO2 highly recommended.

Message me with any questions you may have.

Please fill out the 2026 TORC ride waiver. The link is below. It only needs to be filled out 1 time per year.

https://www.webscorer.com/register?raceid=415052

**HOW TO HELP TORC HELP YOU:**
If you aren't a member of TORC please consider joining. Trails are not cheap to build or easy to maintain. So much goes on behind the scenes at all the trails. If you love trails please consider joining TORC to help support the work TORC does. You may join TORC at https://www.torc-nc.org/join-torc/

Also please consider donating to Triangle Land Conservancy (TLC). https://www.triangleland.org/give/donate

P.S. All the cool kids wear mismatched socks on Trail Tuesday.

title: Price Cone Liptzin Lecture with Guy Mossman
location: Carroll Hall, Knight Learning Lab (Carroll Hall 111)
description:
Hosted by the UNC Hussman School of Journalism and Media, the fall 2026 Price Cone Liptzin Lecture will feature alumnus Guy Mossman ’04 (M.A.), an American cinematographer whose work bridges intimate character study with bold, cinematic visuals.

 

Mossman made his first short film while serving in the Peace Corps in Paraguay in 2000 and went on to earn a Park Fellowship at UNC-Chapel Hill, completing a master’s degree focused on journalism and documentary filmmaking. 

 

He is known for his dramatic, natural-light photography on award-winning documentaries including the Oscar-shortlisted Sundance Audience Award winner “Buck,” the Sundance Special Jury Prize-winning “Feels Good Man” and “Bending the Arc.”

 

In 2022, he made his directorial debut co-directing and lensing “The Human Trial,” an ambitious, years-long chronicle of a radical Type 1 diabetes clinical trial. Most recently, he co-directed, produced and photographed SPEAK., a feature documentary that premiered at the 2025 Sundance Film Festival, following teenage competitive orators at the National Speech & Debate Association’s championship as they discover the power of their voices through oratory and storytelling.

 

Registration

RSVP on Eventbrite

UNC students can register for CLE credit on Heel Life

 

About Mary Jane Price and Annie Cone Liptzin

The visual communication alumni-in-residence series was created in honor of Mary Jane Price and Annie Cone Liptzin, alumnae who volunteered for nearly a decade to assist with the darkroom, equipment checkout and other needs of the UNC Hussman visual journalism program beginning in the 1980s.

title: Travel CHINA like a local! Virtual QnA [x-posted]
description:
Raleigh & Triangle Activities Meetup Group
Putting out feelers for curious, cooperative 'comrades' to explore quiet corners of Old Cathay! Trip date TBD - waiting for airfares to come down.

This will happen on Google Meet.

**CHECK THE COMMENTS FOR MEETING LINK!**

[Comment if you are able to log onto the link but don't see me - in the past Google has let two meetings with the same link open, each person thinking the other didn't show up. So comment here and we'll see if we can fix it. :-) ]

I've been traveling to China for 27 years. Join me for a unique, off the beaten track culture immersion adventure!

Comfort NOT guaranteed! LOTS of walking! This trip is NOT for everyone but everyone who has come with me so far has LOVED it!

Itinerary NOT guaranteed so as to maximize experience! Spontaneous private zheng concert in a riverside pavilion? Let's stop and enjoy! Weather is forecast to be rain in the mountains? Let's go to the ancient village instead.

Costs currently unknown but should be under $100/day for ALL in-country necessities: food, lodging, entrance fees, ground transport. Whatever price I end up quoting will NOT include transport to/from China, alcohol, upgrades to lodging\*, upgrades to in-country transport\*.

You can do it cheaper with a big box tour. If strict time schedules, overpriced shopping, industrial restaurant food, and being kept away from locals is good enough for you than that's your best bet. If unique, real China, great food, insider knowledge with eye for western comforts\*\*, and turn on a dime\*\*\* [a mao?] escapades are for you than come with me!

Only seven people! Small and 'nimble'\*\*\*!

Have you already been to China? Already have seen the Forbidden City and Great Wall? No worries! Big box tours do NOT go where I go!

Have you never been to China and NEED to see the big sights? No problem! I can create an optional 3 day add-on for the Great Wall, Forbidden City, Temple of Heaven, and other Beijing highlights. AND I can take you to hidden gems few big tours touch.

Let's dialog! Looking for like minded people so everyone's on the same page. Don't want to put hard-core shoppers with shop-hating history buffs, or long distance hikers with casual strollers. Just a more practical way to go. If enough interest I can lead TWO trips, each with its own emphasis. I reserve the right to group/accept/deny as I see fit. [I only want happiness! Sometimes that means saying 'maybe next time'.]

Go to Jan Tu Tours on FB and browse the photo albums to get a hint of what one might see. No guarantees of ANYTHING! China changes very quickly.

\*Where available - LOTS of things NOT available off the beaten track. I said 'adventure'!

\*\*Sometimes western comforts are just not there. Deep in the countryside villages rarely have western toilets.

\*\*\*Quick change of plans is relative in China; western expectations are best set aside and an embrace the new/unknown/surprise attitude is highly recommended. But that's what a cultural adventure is all about!

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words
description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026

This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.

 

An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.

Refreshments will be served.

Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

**There will be a second celebration of this exhibit on Friday, October 9 (5-7pm) in honor of the 246th Commemoration Weekend of this historical event.**

title: Narrative Analysis for the Qualitative Researcher (online)
description:
This course features Dynamic Narrative Inquiry – theory and principles for narrative research design and analysis drawing on the richness of expressive language. With this approach to qualitative inquiry, researchers can build on communication in daily life where diverse practices for sharing experience, making sense of experience, and imagining social change occur in personal narratives, sociocultural communications, and institutional policies.

This course involves a sequence of presentations and practical workshops with narrative analysis strategies applicable to small or large studies that sample verbal and/or visual discourse. We begin with an introduction to dynamic narrative inquiry, followed by modules with three analysis strategies that yield findings to a wide range of relevant social science research questions. With examples from prior published studies, I present rationales and methodology, including character mapping (to identify meaning in narrative actors, actions, and relationships); plot analysis (to identify how narrative structures express logics and intentions); and values analysis (to identify speaker/author/ purposes). The final hour of the day is devoted to discussing course participants’ insights from the workshops and implications for future research, practice, and policy.

Registration and fee (refundable for students) are required for Zoom link.

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

We’ll kick things off at the Marshall Public Library with a program led by ATC’s NNIP specialist, Emily Powell. After lunch, we’ll head to the Appalachian Trail just outside of Hot Springs and apply our knowledge in the field. This is a great opportunity to learn about the different invasive plant species in Western North Carolina and effective strategies for removal. Post-training we will discuss opportunities to contribute to the invasive removal effort along the AT. 
Invasive plant species form dense monocultures, crowding out native vegetation and reducing biodiversity. Invasive plant species removal is a critical step in promoting a well-rounded ecosystem. By taking action to control and eradicate invasive plant species, we can help protect native biodiversity, restore ecosystem and trail functionality, and ensure a healthier and more balanced natural world for both people and wildlife.

title: Managing The Emotions Surrounding Layoff Conversations
description:
Delivering layoff messages generates a range of emotions for both the manager delivering the message and the employee receiving it. As a manager, you may feel guilt over having to be the bearer of such bad news. You may feel fear from many sources: fear about your own job security, fear about the impact the announcement will have on others, and fear about how the employee might react during the conversation. Some managers also feel anger, which could be directed toward senior leadership or others responsible for putting managers and the company in this difficult position. All of these emotions are normal and expected. This training helps you better understand these emotions so that you can stay in control of the situation and do your best, instead of allowing the emotions to take over and negatively impact the conversation and your own well-being.

title: Agent Orchestration in the Enterprise: Coordination, Control, and Scale
description:
Data Science Raleigh
As enterprises move from isolated AI assistants to interconnected agentic systems, orchestration is becoming a critical layer of the AI stack. Coordinating multiple agents across tools, data sources, models, and workflows introduces new opportunities for automation—but also new challenges around reliability, governance, observability, and control.

This session explores what it takes to design and operationalize agent orchestration in enterprise environments. From assigning roles and managing handoffs to monitoring performance and enforcing guardrails, we’ll examine how organizations can build coordinated agent systems that scale without sacrificing trust, security, or human oversight.

**You’ll Learn:**

* From Agents to Systems: How orchestration enables multiple agents, models, tools, and workflows to work together toward shared business objectives.
* Coordination and Handoffs: Approaches for assigning tasks, managing dependencies, resolving conflicts, and maintaining context across agents.
* Control and Observability: How to monitor agent behavior, evaluate performance, and intervene when workflows break down or produce unexpected outcomes.
* Scaling Responsibly: Strategies for governing, securing, and scaling agentic systems while maintaining accountability and appropriate human oversight.

**[Register here](https://datasciconnect.com/events/webinars/agent-orchestration-in-the-enterprise-coordination-control-and-scale/)**

title: Kilgour Lecture featuring Hannah Cyrus
description:
Join the School of Data and Information Sciences for the Kilgour Lecture in Information Science, featuring Hannah Cyrus, digital media librarian at Bangor Public Library. Cyrus will present the lecture, “Building Solidarity with Library Patrons through Tech Refusal,” on Wednesday, Oct. 28, from 3:30 to 4:15 p.m. in Carolina Union Room 3411 and via Zoom.

 

A Q&A will take place from 4:15 to 4:30 p.m., followed by a reception and refreshments from 4:30 to 5 p.m. Students can earn CLE credit for attending.

 

The event is open to the public. Register online and indicate whether you plan to attend in person or online.

 

Abstract: 

Library patrons, like library workers, are increasingly expected to make use of digital technologies to work, manage their daily needs, and access information. Frequently, these technologies are delivered by some of the largest, most powerful corporations in the world, and the privacy, mental health and environmental impacts of using them often run counter to the library profession’s stated values. As librarianship requires more and more understanding of digital products, how can librarians, as professionals, connect with patrons, working to build power together in the face of the pressures to adopt different technologies?

 

In this lecture, Hannah Cyrus, Digital Media Librarian at the Bangor Public Library, will share stories from her technology instruction work and explore how libraries are positioned to work with our communities on technology questions. Library workers can build mutual understanding and prioritize patron autonomy through honoring skepticism towards technology, combatting assumptions and dominant narratives around tech, and keeping refusal a viable option. At a time when government agencies are harnessing the mass surveillance infrastructure built by tech companies, AI use is becoming a prerequisite for professional advancement in many fields, and using the internet is feeling less fun than ever, many people are re-thinking their relationships with technology – from returning to flip phones to cutting down license plate reader cameras. As trusted sources of information, library workers can and should be part of these conversations, working with our patrons to meet their needs while holding true to professional values.

 

More about Hannah Cyrus

Hannah Cyrus works as the digital media librarian at Bangor Public Library in Bangor, Maine, with a focus on technology instruction and digital privacy. Her work often centers around patrons concerned about their accounts being compromised, overwhelmed with junk email and spam phone calls, or concerned by the ubiquitous creepiness of online surveillance capitalism. Hannah received her Master of Science in Library & Information Science from Simmons University in 2016. She is a member of the Library Freedom Project and a recipient of the 2026 Jim Campbell Intellectual Freedom Award from the Maine Library Association. Her article, “Refusal as Instruction: Equipping Patrons to Resist AI, Data Brokers, Big Tech, & More,” was published in Information Technology & Libraries in March of 2026.

 

About the OCLC/Frederick G. Kilgour Lecture in Information Science

The Frederick G. Kilgour Lecture was established in 2004 by the Online Computer Library Center (OCLC) on the occasion of Dr. Kilgour’s 90th birthday. Kilgour was a Distinguished Research Professor Emeritus at the School of Information and Library Science (SILS) and Founder of OCLC. Of his many innovations, he is most noted for inventing the WorldCat database in 1971. Today, OCLC is a nonprofit global library cooperative providing shared technology services, original research, and community programs so that libraries can better fuel learning, research and innovation.

title: Teacher Discussion: Unpacking American Indian Heritage Month
description:
Unpacking American Indian Heritage Month
Wed. Oct. 28, 2026 | 6:00–7:00 pm (followed by Q&A)

A free virtual discussion for K-12 educators 

American Indian Heritage Month each November offers a powerful chance for educators to highlight the rich cultures, histories, and ongoing contributions of American Indian communities in North Carolina. In preparation, K–12 educators are invited to join DNCR’s NC American Indian Heritage Commission to deepen essential understandings of contemporary American Indian tribes across the state while dispelling common misconceptions and stereotypes. 

Participants will explore practical ideas, vetted resources, and culturally grounded approaches that support meaningful integration of Native people, stories, and perspectives into classroom instruction, during November and throughout the entire school year.

Educators in attendance can request a .1 CEU form after the event. 

Don’t miss this opportunity to strengthen your practice and ensure your students learn accurate, relevant, and inspiring North Carolina Native narratives all year long.

Registration

Please fill out this form no later than Oct. 28 at Noon to register; a zoom link will be provided via e-mail several days before the event.

Questions?
Contact education.outreach@dncr.nc.gov 

Presenter
Stephen Bell serves as Associate Director of the North Carolina American Indian Heritage Commission within the N.C. Department of Natural and Cultural Resources (DNCR.) In this role, he supports statewide initiatives and partnerships that preserve, interpret, and celebrate American Indian history, arts, customs, and culture. Bell has more than a decade of experience serving students, educators, and communities, having begun his career as a middle school science teacher and later serving as a school social worker and American Indian Education Coordinator for Guilford County Schools. Bell is a citizen of the Lumbee Tribe of North Carolina. He was named the National Indian Education Association’s National Educator of the Year in 2023 and received the Native American 40 Under 40 Award in 2025.

Learn more about the NC American Indian Heritage Commission at aihc.nc.gov. 

Visit DNCR’s page featuring our K-12 education resources at dncr.k12.nc.gov.

Team ENOUGH is a youth-led program whose mission is to educate young voices about gun violence and mobilize them to take meaningful action against it. Supported by Brady United, we harness the expertise and experience of today’s youth to advance our intersectional work across the country. 

Led by an Executive Council, comprised of students just like us, we believe that diversity is a strength, and that only when everyone has a seat at the table can we build an effective movement to prevent all gun violence in all communities.

For us, preventing gun violence not only requires regulating access to firearms but also addressing how systemic racism and environmental factors cause this form of bloodshed to run especially rampant in communities of color. You cannot talk about gun violence without talking about police brutality, white supremacy, the broken criminal justice system, poverty, homophobia, access to affordable housing, or the often barriers separating disadvantaged populations from physical and mental healthcare. 

So if you share this belief, join us for our Team ENOUGH welcome session and become part of the movement to end gun violence in our lifetime.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and artist conversation: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light is an exhibition of seven works by multidisciplinary artist taylor barnes, created during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. Weight of Light considers the relationship between material, perception, and the ongoing process of becoming. Emerging from a period of experimentation and personal reflection, the works occupy an ambiguous space between painting and object. Neither fixed representations nor resolved compositions, the works function as thresholds—sites of transition where questions of origin, transformation, and self-possession remain open.

 

barnes approaches the canvas as a material structure rather than a passive surface. Through staining, layering, saturation, and the transformation of matter between solid and liquid states, she explores the physical and conceptual possibilities of charcoal. Materials shift, settle, resist, and respond, creating conditions in which chance, absence, and emergence become integral to the work. The works do not seek resolution through conventional notions of completion. Instead, they retain evidence of their making—gestures, interruptions, accumulations, and erasures that reveal the instability and possibility inherent in transformation. What remains visible is a record of decisions, encounters, and material negotiations. The works resist linear narratives of progress, suggesting instead a cyclical understanding of origin, movement, and revelation. Abstract maps, they trace an unfolding relationship between the known and obscured. Darkness and light emerge not as opposing forces, but as interdependent conditions which continually refigure perception and understanding. Black, the central color and philosophical foundation of barnes' practice, becomes a space of depth, presence, and possibility—a means of considering how material holds identity, memory, and lived experience. Informed by bell hooks' writings on objectification and subjectivity, barnes' work engages questions of agency, visibility, and the reclamation of self. Ultimately, Weight of Light proposes ascension not as transcendence or arrival, but as an ongoing practice of self-possession. Through material experimentation and an embrace of uncertainty, barnes creates space for the possibility that becoming is neither linear nor complete, but continually negotiated through acts of making, unmaking, and reclamation.

 

taylor barnes is a multidisciplinary artist working across ceramics, fibers, and drawing. Her practice investigates spirituality, oral history, and structures of power through material and form. Working primarily with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal, she translates emotion and lived experience into material forms that hold traces of labor, memory, and ritual. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

Artist website: https://www.barnesartistry.com/ 

 

For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

title: Guided Tour and Meditation with Maya Freelon
description:
Join artist Maya Freelon for an immersive gallery tour of Grounded, exploring the evolution of her work, creative practice, and the Freelon lineage and legacy. Through conversation, "slow looking", gentle movement, awareness, and discovery, participants will engage with the textures, colors, materials, and memories embedded in Freelon’s work.

The tour will include artwork by Maya Freelon, alongside photographs by her late father, Phil Freelon — NC State Design School alum and architect of the renovated Gregg Museum of Art & Design — and her great-grandfather, Allan Freelon, Sr., a pioneer African American Impressionist painter active during the Harlem Renaissance.

The exhibition space welcomes the practice of grounding, as Maya guides visitors through mindful moments that evoke the senses and invite reflection on ancestry, healing, joy, resilience, and connection. description:
Join NCWF Swannanoa Valley WILD! and Highland Farms as they welcome NCWF Conservation Manager, Luke Bennett. North Carolina Wildlife Federation in partnership with National Parks Conservation Association, Center for Biological Diversity, Defenders of Wildlife, MountainTrue, Southern Appalachian Highlands Conservancy, and NCWRC, with support from the U.S. Forest Service, implemented a cerulean warbler and avian diversity survey focused on the last remaining patches of old-growth forests and maturing second-growth forests within our study area – the Craggy Mountains – a 16,000 acre portion of Pisgah National Forest where the presence of cerulean warblers and other avian species is largely unknown. 
Our goal was to fill area-specific knowledge gaps through science-based data collection to assist with future forest management decision-making and conservation efforts. The survey results will be used to educate and inspire the birding and non-birding public on Southern Appalachian neotropical bird migrant diversity, causes of decline, and opportunities for increased protections. Further, there’s an opportunity to support the designation of the Craggy Mountains as a National Scenic Area. 
Join us for a presentation as we discuss the project and highlight ways to get involved!

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and artist conversation: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light is an exhibition of seven works by multidisciplinary artist taylor barnes, created during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. Weight of Light considers the relationship between material, perception, and the ongoing process of becoming. Emerging from a period of experimentation and personal reflection, the works occupy an ambiguous space between painting and object. Neither fixed representations nor resolved compositions, the works function as thresholds—sites of transition where questions of origin, transformation, and self-possession remain open.

 

barnes approaches the canvas as a material structure rather than a passive surface. Through staining, layering, saturation, and the transformation of matter between solid and liquid states, she explores the physical and conceptual possibilities of charcoal. Materials shift, settle, resist, and respond, creating conditions in which chance, absence, and emergence become integral to the work. The works do not seek resolution through conventional notions of completion. Instead, they retain evidence of their making—gestures, interruptions, accumulations, and erasures that reveal the instability and possibility inherent in transformation. What remains visible is a record of decisions, encounters, and material negotiations. The works resist linear narratives of progress, suggesting instead a cyclical understanding of origin, movement, and revelation. Abstract maps, they trace an unfolding relationship between the known and obscured. Darkness and light emerge not as opposing forces, but as interdependent conditions which continually refigure perception and understanding. Black, the central color and philosophical foundation of barnes' practice, becomes a space of depth, presence, and possibility—a means of considering how material holds identity, memory, and lived experience. Informed by bell hooks' writings on objectification and subjectivity, barnes' work engages questions of agency, visibility, and the reclamation of self. Ultimately, Weight of Light proposes ascension not as transcendence or arrival, but as an ongoing practice of self-possession. Through material experimentation and an embrace of uncertainty, barnes creates space for the possibility that becoming is neither linear nor complete, but continually negotiated through acts of making, unmaking, and reclamation.

 

taylor barnes is a multidisciplinary artist working across ceramics, fibers, and drawing. Her practice investigates spirituality, oral history, and structures of power through material and form. Working primarily with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal, she translates emotion and lived experience into material forms that hold traces of labor, memory, and ritual. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

title: NC Public Librarian Certification Commission
description:
The NC Public Librarian Certification Commission was formed in 1936 to set minimum standards for public librarians to protect and maintain public library resources, to assure professional management and administration of library services, to meet the personnel requirements for State Aid administered by the Library of NC, and to guarantee the best possible public library service to all North Carolinians.

The North Carolina General Statute 143B-68 states that the commission must be comprised of: the Chairman of the public libraries section of NCLA, two individuals named by the Governor upon nomination of the NCLA, the dean of a State or regionally accredited graduate school of librarianship in North Carolina appointed by the Governor, and one member at large appointed by the Governor. Commission members appointed by the Governor serve 4-year terms, all others serve 2-year terms.

Commission meetings are held quarterly to review applications and discuss Certification policies and procedures.

The commission's meeting dates for the 2025-2026 year are October 27, 2025, January 9, 2026, April 10, 2026, and July 10, 2026. All meetings are held at the Library of NC beginning at 1:00 pm unless otherwise posted. Information about meetings can be found on the North Carolina Secretary of State's meeting calendar.

Have questions about certification? Contact us at NC.Certification.Commission@dncr.nc.gov.

title: IAH Fellows Forum: Antonia Randolph
description:
On Oct. 30, American studies Assistant Professor Antonia Randolph (FFP ’22) will give a Fellows Forum presentation titled “It’s All Love? Beyoncé and Jay-Z and the Re-enchantment of Black Romance in the Age of the Manosphere.”

 

This talk will examine Jay-Z and Beyoncé’s post-2010 output, with an emphasis on Everything Is Love (The Carters, 2018) and Renaissance (Beyoncé, 2022), to show how their defense of romantic love converts their need to salvage their brand as hip-hop and R&B’s happily married power couple into a story about saving the Black nation through heteronormative marriage.

 

To satisfy R&B audiences, they infuse their marriage with Black nationalist significance, with its survival serving as a proxy for the survival of the Black nation. They link social mobility and wealth with heteronormative marriage, simultaneously turning marriage into an aspirational luxury item while encouraging people to look to marriage, rather than the state, to escape poverty.

 

At the same time, they satisfy hip-hop’s norms by constructing Beyoncé as uniquely deserving of empathy as the ultimate “ride or die” chick, denying that other Black women deserve the care and consideration she receives. These individualized, anti-redistributive responses to shifting gender norms and the erosion of the social safety net in the post-Civil Rights Era provide a cultural commonsense that supports the Black manosphere.

 

Antonia Randolph is the Jonathan M. Hess Career Development Term Assistant Professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Her interests include diversity discourse in education, Black feminist thought, non-normative Black masculinity and sexuality, and hip-hop culture. Her book, The Wrong Kind of Different: Challenging the Meaning of Diversity in American Classrooms (Teachers College Press, 2012), examined the hierarchies elementary school teachers constructed among students of color. Her current book project, That’s My Heart: Queering Intimacy in Hip-Hop Culture, forthcoming from the University of California Press, examines portrayals of Black men’s intimate relationships in hip-hop culture.
